args.text: [lane-heron] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to old servers after a move or failover, causing outages. (2) Slow security fixes: a poisoned or wrong answer stays in the cache longer, and revoking a bad record takes longer. (3) Slow changes: planned migrations and traffic shifts take longer to roll out, with figures such as delay length unknown.

[lane-heron] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that hide whether a request worked, so callers must try again. If repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once, a retry cannot cause double charges, duplicate orders or other harmful repeats.

[lane-heron] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a time-ordered unique identifier) as a primary key: (1) Good: because values rise with time, new rows land near the end of the index, so inserts are faster and pages are used better than with random UUIDs. (2) Bad: the identifier carries its creation time and is larger than a plain integer (16 bytes against 4 or 8), so it leaks when a row was made and makes indexes bigger.

[lane-heron] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to durable storage before it changes the main data, so every change is saved first as a simple list of steps. After a crash, the system replays this list to restore a consistent state, which stops half-finished changes from corrupting data and lets the main files be written more lazily.

[lane-heron] (1) A client version can change how fast requests are sent, retried or batched, so pinning it means any change in results comes from the thing being tested, not from the tool. (2) Pinning lets other people repeat the run later and get comparable figures, because the same client behaves the same way each time.

[lane-heron] Backpressure is a signal that tells the senders of work to slow down or stop when a queue is filling faster than the receivers can empty it. It keeps the queue from growing without limit, which protects memory and keeps waiting times predictable, instead of letting the system fail under overload.

[lane-heron] A cron job can run twice in two ways: (1) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts, so the two overlap; (2) the same schedule is installed on two servers, or a restart or clock change fires the job again. One guard is a lock, for example a lock file or database lock that the job must take before it starts, so a second copy exits straight away.

[lane-heron] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item, so that every copy of the store learns the item was removed. Without it, a copy that missed the delete could send the old value back and bring the item to life again. Tombstones are kept for a set time, then cleared away.

[lane-heron] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than truly failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change between runs; (2) it fails only under certain conditions, such as slow machines, a particular order of tests, or a busy network, and passes when run again on its own.

[lane-heron] A lease-based lock lets one holder act until a set expiry time. If the holder's clock runs slow compared with the lock service's clock, it believes it still holds the lease after the service has given it to someone else. Two holders then act together, which breaks the exclusion the lock was meant to give.
